# HealthQueue observability plan

Goal: know - from data, not guesses - whether patients can book appointments, and decide with the error budget
when to ship faster or slow down.

* Workbook: [`reports/slo-error-budget.xlsx`](../reports/slo-error-budget.xlsx) (generated by
  `scripts/build_slo_workbook.py`; all numbers are formulas, 14 independent checks).
* Alert rules: [`observability/prometheus/slo-rules.yaml`](../observability/prometheus/slo-rules.yaml), unit-tested by
  [`tests/prometheus/slo-rules.test.yaml`](../tests/prometheus/slo-rules.test.yaml) with `promtool`.
* Incident runbook: [`runbooks/incident-api-availability.md`](runbooks/incident-api-availability.md).

> **Data labels.** The 30-day month in the workbook is **SYNTHETIC** (simulated). The `Observed_Local` sheet is
> **real measurement of the real code on a laptop kind cluster** for ~90 seconds - useful evidence that the
> instrumentation works, but not production reliability.

## 1. SLIs and SLOs

The SLO targets are a **design decision** proposed by the engineering team - the assignment does not mandate
them. 99.9% is a common, defensible starting point for a patient-facing booking API run by a small team in one
region; 99.99% would allow only 4.3 minutes of downtime a month, which a startup with one on-call engineer cannot
honestly promise. Targets should be reviewed after 3 months of real data.

| SLI | Good events (numerator) | Eligible events (denominator) | Not eligible | Window | Success criterion | SLO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Availability** (request-based) | `/v1/*` requests answered with status < 500 | all `/v1/*` requests | `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics` | 30-day rolling | status < 500 | **99.9%** |
| **Availability** (time-based) | minutes in which the external probe succeeded | all minutes (43,200) | announced maintenance | 30-day rolling | probe 200 in < 2 s | **99.9%** |
| **Latency** | `/v1/*` requests finished in < 300 ms (server-side) | all `/v1/*` requests | operational endpoints | 30-day rolling | duration < 0.3 s | **99%** |
| **Successful valid submissions** | valid `POST /v1/appointments` answered **201** (booked) or **409** (slot taken - a correct answer) | created + conflict + server error | **422** validation rejections (the client's mistake, not ours) | 30-day rolling | outcome ∈ {created, conflict} | **99.5%** |

Why 4xx counts as *good* for availability: a 404 for an unknown appointment or a 422 for a bad request means the
service worked correctly. Counting them as failures would let a misbehaving client burn our budget.

### PromQL (what Prometheus actually computes)

```promql
# Availability
sum(rate(healthqueue_http_requests_total{route=~"/v1/.*",status!~"5.."}[30d]))
  / sum(rate(healthqueue_http_requests_total{route=~"/v1/.*"}[30d]))

# Latency: the histogram has a bucket at exactly 0.3 s so this is exact, not interpolated
sum(rate(healthqueue_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/v1/.*",le="0.3"}[30d]))
  / sum(rate(healthqueue_http_request_duration_seconds_count{route=~"/v1/.*"}[30d]))

# Successful valid submissions
sum(increase(healthqueue_appointment_submissions_total{outcome=~"created|conflict"}[30d]))
  / sum(increase(healthqueue_appointment_submissions_total{outcome=~"created|conflict|error"}[30d]))
```

Labels use the **route template** (`/v1/appointments/{appointment_id}`), never the raw URL, so metrics stay
low-cardinality and no appointment ID ends up in Prometheus (tested in `tests/test_observability.py`).

## 2. Error budget arithmetic

**Time-based (minutes of downtime):**

```
minutes in 30 days        = 30 x 24 x 60      = 43,200 min
allowed downtime at 99.9% = 43,200 x (1-0.999) = 43.2 min   (0.72 h)
```

**Request-based (failed requests) - a different unit, never mixed with minutes:**

```
allowed failed requests = eligible requests x (1 - SLO)
synthetic September     = 1,036,462 x 0.001 = 1,036.5 failed requests allowed
```

A burst of 900 failed requests in 3 minutes uses 87% of the *request* budget but only 7% of the *time* budget.
That is why the workbook keeps both rows separately.

### Synthetic September 2026 results (from the workbook)

| SLI | Allowed | Consumed | Used | Remaining | State (policy) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Availability (request) | 1,036.5 failed requests | 952 | 91.9% | 8.1% | **FREEZE risky releases** |
| Availability (time) | 43.2 min | 31 min | 71.8% | 28.2% | CAUTION |
| Latency < 300 ms | 10,364.6 slow requests | 5,078 | 49.0% | 51.0% | HEALTHY |
| Valid submissions | 311.0 failed bookings | 189 | 60.8% | 39.2% | CAUTION |

Three synthetic incidents drive this: INC-201 PostgreSQL failover (12 Sep, 22 bad minutes), INC-202 slow query
(19 Sep, latency), INC-203 bad config rolled back by `git revert` (25 Sep, 9 bad minutes).

### Real local measurement (Observed_Local sheet)

| | v0.1.0 (new DB connection per request) | v0.1.1 (connection pool) |
|---|---|---|
| Availability SLI | 100% | 100% |
| Latency SLI (server ≤ 300 ms) | **85.4% - would breach the 99% SLO** | **100%** |
| Submission SLI | 100% | 100% |
| p50 / p95 / p99 (client) | 210 / 403 / 502 ms | 64 / 117 / 157 ms |

This is the observability loop in action: the latency SLI exposed a real design flaw, the fix was shipped through
the full pipeline (Trivy, SBOM, Cosign) and rolled out by a GitOps commit, and the SLI was re-measured.

## 3. Error budget policy

| Budget remaining | State | What the team does |
|---|---|---|
| ≥ 50% | HEALTHY | Ship normally, including planned risky work. |
| 25-50% | CAUTION | Risky changes need a second reviewer and a rollback plan; deploy in business hours; top reliability ticket goes into the next sprint. |
| 0-25% | FREEZE risky releases | Only low-risk changes, bug fixes and reliability work; canary verification on every deploy; postmortem actions take priority. |
| < 0% | EXHAUSTED | Feature releases stop until the rolling window recovers; only fixes/security/reliability ship; CTO is informed. |

Applied per SLO: if only latency is in FREEZE, performance-risky changes pause while unrelated changes continue.
Security fixes may always ship. The policy is reviewed monthly with product.

## 4. Metrics

| Metric | Type | Labels | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `healthqueue_http_requests_total` | counter | method, route, status | availability SLI, traffic, error rate |
| `healthqueue_http_request_duration_seconds` | histogram (buckets incl. 0.3) | method, route | latency SLI, p50/p95/p99 |
| `healthqueue_appointment_submissions_total` | counter | outcome = created / conflict / rejected_validation / error | submission SLI, business KPI |
| `up{job="healthqueue-api"}` | gauge (Prometheus) | - | total-outage detection |
| Kubernetes: restarts, CPU/memory vs limits, ready replicas | kube-state-metrics / cAdvisor (production) | - | saturation, capacity |

The four golden signals are covered: **traffic** (request rate), **errors** (5xx ratio), **latency** (histogram),
**saturation** (CPU/memory vs limits, DB pool usage - pool metrics are a planned addition).

## 5. Logs

* One JSON object per line on stdout (12-factor), e.g.
  `{"ts": "...", "level": "INFO", "msg": "request completed", "request_id": "...", "trace_id": "...", "route": "/v1/appointments", "status": 201, "duration_ms": 14.8}`
* `request_id` is taken from `X-Request-ID` only if it matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{8,64}$` (prevents log injection),
  otherwise generated, and always returned to the client so support can find a request.
* Production: shipped by the node's log agent (Fluent Bit) to CloudWatch Logs - the KMS-encrypted log group is in
  OpenTofu with 90-day retention.

## 6. Traces

OpenTelemetry SDK with FastAPI auto-instrumentation. Each request gets a span; the `trace_id` is written into every
log line so logs and traces can be joined. Export is **off by default** (no external service, $0); set
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to send spans to an OpenTelemetry Collector (production: collector -> Jaeger/Tempo or
AWS X-Ray). Health/metrics endpoints are excluded from tracing to avoid noise.

## 7. Dashboards

One SLO dashboard per service (Grafana in production; the Excel `Dashboard` sheet mirrors it):
1. Budget remaining per SLO (bar) and state (HEALTHY/CAUTION/FREEZE/EXHAUSTED).
2. Burn rate over 1h and 6h windows.
3. Request rate, 5xx ratio, p50/p95/p99 latency per route.
4. Booking outcomes (created / conflict / rejected / error).
5. Pods ready, restarts, CPU/memory vs limits.

## 8. Alerting (multi-window, multi-burn-rate)

Method from the Google SRE Workbook, *Alerting on SLOs*. Burn rate = how many times faster than "exactly on budget"
we are spending. 14.4x for one hour = 2% of the monthly budget gone.

| Alert | Condition | Severity | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HealthQueueAvailabilityFastBurn` | error ratio > 14.4 x 0.1% over 1h **and** 5m, for 2m | page | budget gone in ~2 days |
| `HealthQueueAvailabilitySlowBurn` | > 6x over 6h **and** 30m, for 15m | page | 5% of budget in 6 h |
| `HealthQueueAvailabilityBudgetDrain` | > 1x over 3d **and** 6h, for 1h | ticket | steady leak, fix in hours |
| `HealthQueueLatencyFastBurn` / `SlowBurn` | slow ratio > 14.4 x 1% / 6 x 1% | page / ticket | latency SLO |
| `HealthQueueSubmissionFailuresFastBurn` | failed-submission ratio > 14.4 x 0.5% | page | patients cannot book |
| `HealthQueueApiDown` | `up == 0` for 2m | page | ratios are blind when there is no traffic |

The short window (5m/30m) makes alerts **reset quickly** after recovery; the long window prevents paging on a
blip. Tested with `promtool test rules`: healthy traffic -> no alert; 5% errors -> page; a 3-minute blip -> no page;
target down -> page; 10% booking failures -> page. Every alert links to the runbook.

## 9. Privacy controls (health data)

* The API accepts **no direct identifiers** - no names, DOB, phone, address or free-text notes; `extra="forbid"`
  rejects unknown fields (tested: a `notes` field with a diagnosis is rejected and not echoed).
* Validation errors return field names and reasons, **never submitted values**.
* Request/response bodies are never logged; metrics labels never contain IDs; exceptions log the type only,
  not the message.
* `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on every response.
* Log retention is bounded (90 days production) and the log group is KMS-encrypted.
* Before handling real PHI, see the checklist in [production-readiness.md](production-readiness.md).

## 10. Runbook and incident process

* Alert -> on-call follows [incident-api-availability.md](runbooks/incident-api-availability.md): check
  rollout history, roll back with `git revert`, check DB, communicate.
* Every page-worthy incident gets a **blameless postmortem** within 5 working days
  ([template and example](postmortems/2026-09-12-inc-201-postgres-failover.md)); its action items are prioritised
  according to the error budget policy above.
